byKey.l: You compared the tops alone. Cross multiply: $11 \times 13 = 143$ against $9 \times 16 = 144$.
byKey.e: Both are close to 0.69, but 143 and 144 differ: $\tfrac{9}{13}$ is larger by $\tfrac{1}{208}$.

explain.text: $11 \times 13 = 143$ and $9 \times 16 = 144$. The right side’s product is larger, so $\tfrac{9}{13}$ wins, by $\tfrac{1}{208}$.

items.question: What is the net change, in percent?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two growth factors.

byKey.added: You added +30% and −30%. The fall acts on the higher price.
byKey.ten: −1% is the answer for 10% each way. With 30% the loss is $0.3^2 = 9\%$.

explain.text: The factors are 1.3 and 0.7, and $1.3 \times 0.7 = 0.91$. Up and down by the same $p$ always loses $p^2$: here $0.09$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round 6.8 up to 7 and 410 down to 400.

byKey.both-up: You rounded both up, to 7 and 420. Round one up and one down.
byKey.power: You lost a power of ten. $7 \times 400 = 2800$.

explain.text: 6.8 rounds up by 3% and 410 down by 2.4%, so $7 \times 400 = 2800$ is 0.4% high. The exact product is 2,788.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $11^2 = 121$, one more than 120.

byKey.halved: You halved 120. Its root is near 11, since $11^2 = 121$.
byKey.ten: $10^2 = 100$ is well short. 120 sits just under $11^2 = 121$.
byKey.no-double: You divided the −1 by 11. Divide by $2 \times 11 = 22$.

explain.text: 120 is $11^2 - 1$, so the step is $-\tfrac{1}{22}$: $\sqrt{120} \approx 10.955$. The true root is 10.954.

items.question: By how much is $\tfrac56$ bigger than $\tfrac45$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the cross-product gap over $6 \times 5$.

byKey.count: 1 is the cross-product gap, or $\tfrac{5 - 4}{6 - 5}$. Divide the gap by 30.

explain.text: $5 \times 5 = 25$ and $4 \times 6 = 24$. The gap of 1 sits over $6 \times 5 = 30$, so the difference is $\tfrac{1}{30}$.

items.prose: A savings rate rises from 2.5% to 3%.
items.question: By what percent did the rate rise?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change in points by the old rate.

byKey.points: 0.5 is the change in points. Divide it by the old rate, 2.5.
byKey.new-base: You divided by the new rate, 3. Measure from the old rate.

explain.text: The rate rose half a percentage point. Half a point on 2.5 is $\tfrac{0.5}{2.5} = 0.2$, a rise of 20%.

items.prose: The interviewer wants the exact figure this time.
items.question: What is $0.51 \times 640$ exactly?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Half of 640, plus 1% of 640.

byKey.half: 320 is half of 640. 0.51 is a half plus 0.01, so add 1% of 640, which is 6.4.
byKey.subtracted: You took the 1% off. 0.51 is above a half, so add it.

explain.text: $0.51 = 0.5 + 0.01$, so the product is $320 + 6.4 = 326.4$. The estimate 320 was 2% low; the exact answer took one more step.

items.prose: Move the point two places to reach a whole number first.
items.question: Estimate $\sqrt{0.3}$ to two decimal places.

byKey.one-place: That is $\sqrt3 \div 10$, the root of 0.03. Moving the point two places in 0.3 gives 30.
byKey.halved: You halved 0.3. Below 1 a root is bigger than its number.

items.question: What percentage rise takes it back to where it was?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the loss by what is left.

byKey.same: You reused 25%. A quarter of the lower value is not enough.
byKey.fall-rule: You used $\tfrac{p}{1+p}$, which undoes a rise. After a loss, divide by $1 - p$.

explain.text: From £100, a 25% fall leaves £75. Getting £25 back is $\tfrac{25}{75}$ of £75, a rise of 33.33%.

items.prose: Two quotes on the same event: 4 to 7 and 5 to 9. You stake £63 at the better one.
items.question: What profit does it pay, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the bigger fraction, then scale it to £63.

byKey.worse: £35 is the 5 to 9 quote. $\tfrac47$ is bigger: $4 \times 9 = 36$ against $5 \times 7 = 35$.
byKey.stake-back: You added back the £63 stake. Give the profit alone.

explain.text: Cross multiplying, 36 beats 35, so 4 to 7 pays more. On £63 it pays $63 \div 7 \times 4 = 36$ pounds. The other quote pays £35.
